A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Re-Schedule research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original training analyses, evaluations of two Qwen2.5 models on six mathematical benchmarks, and ablations in Section 7 and Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds computational-cost measurements, sensitivity studies, repeated-seed results, Qwen3 evaluations, and a coding experiment.

M1.justification: The default tree construction, r-score calculation, and weighted GRPO procedure remain unchanged. Appendix D.6 adds an experimental dynamic variant that regenerates reasoning trees and recomputes scores three times during training. This is a limited procedural extension; offline scoring remains the default.

E1.justification: v1 uses mathematical reasoning data exclusively. v2 retains that coverage and adds code-generation training on ArcherCodeR and evaluation on LiveCodeBench v5 in Appendix D.7, substantially extending the task and domain coverage.

E2.justification: The comparator membership in the original main benchmarks is unchanged, including Eurus-PRIME only for Qwen2.5-Math-7B. New controlled comparisons introduce Reverse Schedule in Table 6 and dynamically refreshed scoring in Table 14. The revised SimpleRL-Zoo scores do not establish a changed comparison method.

E3.justification: v2 introduces Qwen3-4B-Base evaluations and a DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B coding protocol reporting pass@1 and pass@4 using eight samples. It also adds controlled sweeps of token interval, branching factor, depth, and modification budget, plus ordering and refresh-frequency controls. These substantially expand the experimental design without establishing changes to the retained main training recipe.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained analyses, v2 adds computational cost versus performance, easy-to-hard versus reversed ordering, token-interval sensitivity, separately controlled branching/depth sweeps, modification-budget sensitivity, and static versus refreshed scoring. These test important design and robustness questions absent from v1. The original Fix-versus-Pruning ablation is retained as Appendix D.1/Table 7.

E5.justification: Appendix D.2 newly reports repetitions with different random seeds and Table 8 presents six benchmark results as Avg. ± Var. v1 contains no corresponding training-run uncertainty report. The addition is limited to Re-Schedule; run counts, seed identities, baseline variances, and formal significance tests remain unspecified.

E6.justification: SimpleRL-Zoo's numerical rows change in Tables 1 and 2, including averages of 44.0 to 44.6 and 39.8 to 40.0; Re-Schedule's main scores remain unchanged. Substantial new results include Qwen3 averages of 48.8 versus ACC's 46.6 and GRPO's 44.5, coding pass@1/pass@4 of 26.3/37.8 versus GRPO's 25.4/35.4, and the added cost, variance, and ablation results. These additions concern newly evaluated settings.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and Equations 1–10, including the reasoning tree, node/query r-scores, and weighting functions, are retained. The MCN definition is also unchanged. No new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same central claims: structural learnability through r-score, an easy-to-hard Re-Schedule curriculum, and accuracy gains up to 3.2% on six mathematical benchmarks. Additional evidence does not redefine these headline contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning preprocessing cost, curriculum ordering, coarse trees at large token intervals, parameter robustness, static scoring sufficiency, and applicability to other models and coding. Some new interpretations overreach: Appendix D.5 claims superiority over ACC across all benchmarks, although Table 13 reports lower AMC23 accuracy, 57.6 versus 59.3.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies avg@32 for mathematical evaluation, the default modification budget M = 10, and timing measurements on eight H20 GPUs with an approximately 46-hour, five-epoch training reference. It also documents coding evaluation details. v1's M = 4 was illustrative, so a budget change is not established. The existing implementation appendix and code-access statement are retained.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands the cited literature, including entropy interventions, reward dithering, LiveCodeBench, and agent/multimodal directions. Section 2.2 also revises LPPO's description from accuracy weighting and online prompts to accuracy gradients, and Seed-GRPO's from token entropy to semantic diversity, sharpening the positioning against outcome-based proxies.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence remain intact. Local revisions clarify related work and the motivation example, update affiliations and conference headers, and add acknowledgements. New analysis subsections and an expanded supplementary-experiment hierarchy are introduced, with the original setup and metric-selection material retained under new appendix labels.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the evidence displays with a cost-performance plot and ten additional tables covering timing, ordering, variance, sensitivity, model transfer, dynamic scoring, and coding. Existing Figures 1–4 and Tables 1–4 are retained, with limited sizing/caption changes; v1's Table 5 becomes Table 7.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support for the expensive, offline scoring design. Cost measurements, ordering controls, independent sensitivity sweeps, and static-versus-dynamic comparisons address important validation gaps in v1; coding and Qwen3 experiments extend applicability evidence. These gains outweigh localized reporting weaknesses, including unspecified repeat counts, inconsistent cost-display labels, and the Table 13 all-benchmarks overclaim. The improvement comes from testing previously unsupported design assumptions and practical tradeoffs, rather than higher headline scores.
